Introduction

Ever since the computer was invented, simulation has been one of its core tasks. In the early days, visual simulation still had a long way to go before it looked realistic, so most research went into simulating graphics and images.

Over the past twenty years, as games and animated films have looked ever more lifelike, users have started to expect realistic sound as well. Research on sound simulation (in this article, “sound” always means environmental sound, not speech or music) has therefore been attracting more attention, giving rise to research areas such as sound synthesis, sound propagation and sound spatialization. Together these feed into the broader field of auralization; see two of our earlier articles:

Exploring auralization in urban design

A history of acoustics: auralization

This article gives a brief introduction to these three main areas and shows some of the latest research from the computer science side. Later articles will look in detail at each of the places where computer science and acoustics meet.

1. Sound synthesis

Sound synthesis, also called sound modeling, is about building digital models of how sound sources produce sound, so as to generate source signals that are as close to the real thing as possible. The main aim is to deliver highly realistic sound in games and virtual reality applications, automatically synchronized with the visual scene.

prosoundnetwork.com

Current sound synthesis methods fall into the four main categories shown in the figure below. Physical models describe the source signal based on the principles of physical acoustics, while signal models use psychoacoustic principles to build source models that are perceptually similar. Hybrid models, which combine physical acoustics with psychoacoustics, and deep learning models have been the hot approaches in recent years.

Figure 1. The main categories of sound synthesis methods

Early research on sound synthesis focused on impact and rolling sounds of solid objects. The sounds in the example below, for instance, were synthesized entirely automatically from the parameters of a physically based motion simulation [4].

Researchers have also explored the sounds produced by solid objects in a range of motion states, such as impact and rolling [5].

As research in the field has deepened, the range of sound scenes that synthesis methods can simulate has steadily grown, from solids with relatively simple vibration behavior to soft bodies, liquids and gases (burning flames) [6].

In the past few years, researchers have begun to explore coupled scenarios. Below are synthesized sounds for liquid–solid interaction, from the author’s own PhD work [7].

2. Sound propagation

Sound propagation simulation means computing a sound field model (comprising the source, the listener and the propagation environment) to obtain the signal that arrives at the listener after traveling from the source. Existing methods for simulating sound propagation fall into three main categories.

Figure 2. The main categories of sound propagation methods [1]

The world’s leading team in sound propagation research is currently the Interactive Media Group at Microsoft Research in Redmond. They are running Project Acoustics, which aims to build an acoustics engine for interactive 3D experiences [9]. Below is a video of the team’s research published in 2020 [3].

3. Sound spatialization

Sound spatialization studies how the human ear perceives and interprets the three-dimensional spatial information carried by a sound signal, and how to convey that sense of space effectively on a computer. Its main research areas include binaural rendering and ambisonics.

In my view, demand from the headphone and loudspeaker industries has driven the rapid growth of this area. Research here began earlier than in the other two areas, and there are also more research groups working on it in China.

cbinsights.com

In short, computer sound simulation is an emerging interdisciplinary field that brings together mathematics, acoustics, computer science and cognitive science. It explores how to process and represent sound information effectively on a computer, along with the theories, models and algorithms for simulating, processing and presenting sound with computers. That sound information includes both the sound of the physical world and the virtual sound perceived by the human brain. Computer sound simulation is the medium that connects these two worlds inside the computer.

About the author: Haonan Cheng is a PhD student in computer science at Tianjin University. His research interests include sound synthesis and computer graphics.
